title: Data Types, Variables & Operators
relevance: Campus OAs and SDE interviews probe C/C++ type sizing, signed/unsigned mixing, and operator pitfalls that silently break loops and bit checks.

phases.goal: Establish C's scalar type system, sizing guarantees, literals, and basic variable rules.

must_hit.point: C is statically typed: every variable and expression has a type known at compile time, which dictates byte count and interpretation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says types are fixed at compile time and control both size and how bits are read.

must_hit.point: The C standard guarantees minimum ranges for integer types, not exact byte sizes; the compiler picks sizes for the target.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions minimum ranges (e.g. int at least 16 bits) and that typical sizes like 4-byte int are platform choices.

must_hit.point: Plain char signedness is implementation-defined; use signed char or unsigned char when math behavior must be specific.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out that plain char may be signed or unsigned depending on the compiler.

must_hit.point: sizeof gives size in bytes; actual min/max limits come from limits.h (INT_MAX, UINT_MAX, etc.) or float.h.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names sizeof plus limits.h/float.h macros rather than hard-coding assumed sizes.

must_hit.point: stdint.h exact-width types (int8_t, uint16_t, int32_t, uint64_t) guarantee bit width; size_t is the unsigned type for sizeof results, array indices, and memory sizes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts portable exact-width types with size_t for sizes and indices.

must_hit.point: A declaration introduces name and type without necessarily allocating (extern int x); a definition declares and allocates (int x).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates extern declaration from a defining int x;.

probes: What does the C standard guarantee about the size of int versus what you typically see on modern systems?
When would you reach for uint32_t or size_t instead of plain int?

hints.1: Think about what is fixed at compile time versus what the platform chooses.
hints.2: Separate minimum standard ranges from typical sizes, then name stdint.h and size_t roles.
hints.3: Say: ranges not exact sizes; int often 32 bits though only required to be at least 16; use int32_t for exact layouts and size_t for sizes/indices; plain char signedness is implementation-defined.

phases.goal: Show how operators, precedence, promotions, and conversions actually rewrite expressions.

must_hit.point: Logical && and || short-circuit: && evaluates the right side only if the left is true; || only if the left is false.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains short-circuit and cites a null-pointer guard pattern.

must_hit.point: Bitwise &, ^, and | bind looser than ==, so flags & MASK == 0 parses as flags & (MASK == 0).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the precedence trap and parenthesizes as (flags & MASK) == 0.

must_hit.point: Binary operators first apply integer promotions (char/short to int, or unsigned int if needed), then usual arithmetic conversions by rank and signedness.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both phases: promotions of small integers, then rank/signedness rules for a common type.

must_hit.point: When signed and unsigned operands have equal rank, the signed operand is converted to unsigned—so comparing int -1 to unsigned 0 can be true because -1 becomes UINT_MAX (typically 4,294,967,295).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks signed-to-unsigned conversion and why -1 > 0u can hold.

must_hit.point: Pre-increment (++x) yields the new value; post-increment (x++) yields the current value then increments.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly distinguishes value produced by ++x versus x++.

must_hit.point: Modifying the same scalar twice without an intervening sequence point is undefined behavior; i = i++ is UB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines sequence points as side-effect boundaries and labels i = i++ as UB.

probes: Why can if (a > b) be true when a is int -1 and b is unsigned int 0?
What does if (flags & MASK == 0) actually mean, and how do you write it safely?

hints.1: Focus on what the compiler does before the operator runs when types disagree.
hints.2: Walk integer promotions, then equal-rank signed/unsigned conversion; separately check & versus == precedence.
hints.3: Say: -1 becomes unsigned max (typically 4,294,967,295) so the comparison is true; flags & MASK == 0 is flags & (MASK == 0), so write ((flags & MASK) == 0).

phases.goal: Choose among plain ints, fixed-width types, size_t, and const versus macros with clear rationale.

must_hit.point: Use int when exact size does not matter (native efficient size); use int32_t (and friends) for hardware, network packets, or file formats; use size_t for memory sizes, byte counts, and array indexing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the three-way split with concrete use cases for each.

must_hit.point: #define macros are untyped text replacement with no block scope; const-qualified variables have a type, respect scope, and cannot be modified after initialization.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts preprocessor text swap versus typed, scoped const.

must_hit.point: Widening casts (e.g. int to long long) are generally safe; narrowing (long to short, or float to int) truncates and can permanently change the value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns that narrowing drops high-order bytes or fractional parts.

probes: When should you use int versus int32_t versus size_t?
What is the practical difference between #define MAX_USERS 100 and const int max_users = 100?

hints.1: Ask what you need: native speed, exact layout, or a size/index.
hints.2: Map int → generic counters, stdint exact-width → wire/hardware layouts, size_t → sizes; then contrast macro text vs typed const.
hints.3: State the three use cases explicitly, then: macros have no type/scope; const is typed, scoped, and immutable after init.

phases.goal: Apply type and operator rules to real loops, bit tests, and initialization bugs.

must_hit.point: Mixing a signed loop index with a size_t bound can break if the index goes negative: comparison converts the signed value to unsigned and yields a huge positive value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the signed index versus size_t size() pitfall and unsigned wrap of a negative i.

must_hit.point: Local variables are not zeroed by default; reading an uninitialized local is undefined behavior because it holds garbage leftover bytes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says locals start uninitialized and reading them is UB.

must_hit.point: In C (unlike C++), a character literal like 'A' has type int, not char.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly notes character literals are int in C.

must_hit.point: Always parenthesize bitwise checks as ((flags & MASK) == 0) to avoid the & versus == precedence bug in real conditionals.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Applies the precedence rule as a coding habit with parentheses.

probes: What goes wrong in for (int i = 0; i < my_vector.size(); i++) if i becomes negative inside the body?
Why is reading an uninitialized local variable dangerous?

hints.1: Think about signed versus unsigned in the loop condition, and about what locals contain before assignment.
hints.2: size() is size_t (unsigned); a negative i converts to a huge unsigned value. Locals hold leftover memory until written.
hints.3: Say: i < size() promotes negative i to unsigned so the loop may not stop; uninitialized locals are garbage and reading them is UB; also parenthesize bitwise tests.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use int for generic counters where exact width does not matter so the compiler can pick a native size; use stdint.h types like int32_t when modeling exact hardware, network packets, or file formats; use size_t for memory sizes, byte counts, and array indexing because it matches sizeof and is large enough for any object size.

#define does untyped preprocessor text replacement and ignores block scope; const int (etc.) is a typed, scoped object the compiler refuses to modify after initialization—prefer const when you want type safety and scoping.

Widening (int to long long) generally preserves values; narrowing (long to short) truncates high-order bytes and can change the value, and casting float to int truncates the fractional part—treat narrowing as dangerous.

gotchas.trap: Assuming plain char is signed (or unsigned) everywhere.
gotchas.correction: Plain char signedness is implementation-defined; use signed char or unsigned char when arithmetic behavior must be fixed.

gotchas.trap: Writing if (flags & MASK == 0) intending a masked equality check.
gotchas.correction: == binds tighter than &, so it becomes flags & (MASK == 0); write if ((flags & MASK) == 0).

gotchas.trap: Believing int a = -1 compared with unsigned int b = 0 yields false for a > b.
gotchas.correction: Equal-rank signed/unsigned usual arithmetic conversions cast -1 to unsigned (typically UINT_MAX 4,294,967,295), so the comparison is true.

gotchas.trap: Reading a local variable before assigning it.
gotchas.correction: Locals are not zero-initialized; they hold garbage, and reading them is undefined behavior—initialize before use.

gotchas.trap: Assuming i = i++ has a defined result.
gotchas.correction: Modifying the same scalar twice with no intervening sequence point is undefined behavior; the compiler may do anything.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a C character literal has type char.
gotchas.correction: In C (unlike C++), 'A' has type int.
